entries.title: Plan writer cost: sub-planners per part, and twill versus a solo writer
entries.brief: The Plan writer is 18% of spend; sub-planners per part for large bundles, and a twill versus solo Opus high comparison on cost, rounds and time
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: the Plan writer is the costliest session type, about $8 per run, $1,306 with its forks over two weeks (18% of all spend).
It averages 81 turns at a mean context of 223k, holds 153k by its first fork and peaks around 308k, mostly from about 71 raw `sed -n`/`grep` code reads.
Every `twill-plan` lens fork inherits that context, about 287k per turn; since 2026-10-20 the writer and its forks cost about $18 per run.

## Idea (orch, not decided)

Fork the lenses earlier, before the code reads pile up, or hand the writer a digest of the code it needs instead of raw reads.
Cutting a quarter of the writer's and its forks' cost saves about 4.5% of all spend; quality must be benched first.

## Discussion with the operator (2026-10-22)

- A code digest instead of raw reads is rejected: it is too inexact unless the code itself is read, and the writer would read the source anyway to be sure.
  Finding what to read is already `relevant.md`'s job; whether the writer uses it is worth measuring (how much of what the writer read the list named).
- Lens forks as fresh agents are rejected: that is the perch itself.
- Sub-planners: Discussion splits the scope into parts in the decision record, groups `relevant.md` per part, and each sub-planner reads only its part; the lead owns the shared spots and joins the card DAG.
  This keeps every review round and matters more as loom tasks are bundled larger.
  Review could split per part the same way, since each fresh reviewer rebuilds its context every round (Plan reviewer: 48 turns at 123k mean context, $2.48 per session).
- Twill-plan versus a solo writer: since the full `twill-plan` fan (2026-10-20), 7 landed loom runs average 2.00 Plan rounds against 2.09 before, while the writer's forks cost about $7 per run and a Plan round about $3.70; too few runs to judge.
  The operator sees strong signs that the twill writer makes a far better one-shot plan in shorter time, and time counts as well as tokens.
  Still, test a solo Opus high writer: compare twill, solo Opus high and solo Fable on Plan cost, Plan rounds and Plan wall time (`lym report timing`) per run.

## Split writing: two variants to bench (operator, 2026-10-22)

Discussion-Write and Plan-Write already run as `shedadapters.MultiLLMProducer` over a `seatengine` table, a chair and advisors; advisors only advise, and twill is the chair forking itself, so today one session writes the whole product.
Two ways to have parts written separately, both benched against each other and against the twill and solo writers before anything reaches production:

1. **Seats with writing assistants.** The chair splits the scope, fixes the interfaces and shared spots, and hands each assistant seat its part; it then joins and checks the parts.
   A new seat role beside the advisor.
   Risks: assistants see neither each other's work nor a shared context, so seams fall to the chair and review, and overlapping parts make several seats read the same code.
2. **Fork-based.** The chair keeps its context lean (scope, split and shared spots only) and forks once per part, so every part writer inherits the same overview without the writer's full reading.
   Technically still one writer with forks, like twill but forking early.

## Data check (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-24)

Plan writer plus its lens forks, means per run (API list price):

| group | runs | writer+forks | forks | Plan-Write wall | Plan rounds |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| before 10-15 (solo writer) | 28 | $9.08 | $0.58 | 16.4 min active | 1.3 |
| 10-15 to 10-19 | 41 | $9.39 | $3.86 | 18.5 min | 1.88 |
| 10-20 to c62274be5 (full twill-plan fan) | 7 | $18.14 | $7.66 | 23.9 min | 2.00 |
| after c62274be5 (five lenses) | 3 | $16.64 | $7.40 | 23.9 min | 1.33 |

- The later groups are larger tasks, so the cost rise is not the fan alone; the five-lens group is too small to judge.
- `relevant.md` use, over 32 runs with a list and a Plan-Write transcript: 85% of named files were read, but only 28% of read files were named (about 3.5 files read per file named, about 7 on large runs). Both shares are lower bounds (directory greps and quarry reads not counted).
- So `relevant.md` works as a floor, not a boundary; most unnamed reading looks like tests and neighbouring callers, which a per-part split of the list would not remove.
- Still open: the solo Opus high and Fable writer bench, and the split-writing variants, which need new runs.
- Scripts, baseline tables and `results.md` are in `docs/research/plan-writer-audit-2026-10-24/`; rerun per its README.

## Discussion versus Plan: double reading (Sonnet agent, 2026-10-25)

55 loom runs seeded 2026-10-15 or later with both a `ly:<slug>:discussion` and a `ly:<slug>:plan` transcript on this machine; cost at API list price from the 10-24 tokencount reports, per run:

| | Discussion | Plan |
|---|---|---|
| phase total (writer, forks, review, fix) | $8.68 | $18.51 |
| writer session alone | $2.07 | $6.60 |
| writer turns / mean context | 39 / 89k tokens | 83 / 183k tokens |
| repo files read by the writer (pooled) | 1,093 | 3,286 |
| share read by both | 62% of Discussion's reads re-read by Plan | 21% of Plan's reads read by Discussion |
| same, without `PATTERN.md`, `CLAUDE.md`, `pattern/`, `docs/` | 64% | 20% |

- Discussion costs 0.47 of Plan for the phase and 0.31 for the writer alone; Discussion was the dearer phase in only 4 of 55 runs.
- Plan-Write re-reads about 62% of the files Discussion-Write read (mean of per-run shares 62%), so exploration is repeated, but Plan reads about three times as many files and most of its reading (79%) is new.
- Rough size of the repeat: the Plan-Write reads that Discussion had already made are about 3.3M tokens pooled, about 59k per run (file bytes at current `main` divided by 4; whole files assumed, so an upper bound).
  That is roughly a third of the Plan writer's mean context, and it is paid again on every later turn through the cache.
- File-level only: directory greps, globs and `lym quarry` reads are not counted, and a file is the same file by path, not by the lines read.
- The Discussion phase total holds its review rounds and fixers, which is most of its cost beyond the writer; the segment figures come from the 10-24 tokencount reports, so runs landed since are priced as of then.
- Rerun: `.scratch/discussion-overlap/reads2.sh <slug> plan|discussion` per run, then `analyze.sh`; both stay in `.scratch` and are not committed.
- Decision (operator, 2026-10-25): Discussion stays a separate step; folding it into the Plan writer would add turns to the costliest session.

## Turn audit (landed 2026-10-28)

`docs/research/turn-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` (n = 1 loom run, 213 sessions) finds the Plan writer spends 33 of its 101 turns on serial single-call reads and searches, mostly shell `grep` and `sed -n`, which a merged turn would remove.
It recommends one stencil sentence in `loom-template-plan.md` and in the twill lens directive: issue every search and read you can name in one message.
This is a cheaper cut than the digest, the earlier fork and the split writing above, and the audit proposes no pre-read for the writer.
The recommendation is untested: no run measured the effect, and the Plan row rests on one session.

entries.title: Large tasks: Discussion, a pre-planner, and the pieces as darn runs inside the task's beam
entries.brief: Discussion decides scope, a pre-planner splits it into contracted pieces, each piece runs as darn from the task's beam, a whole-task perch reviews, then align and land
entries.body:
## Idea (operator, 2026-10-22)

A large task runs as a loom whose implementation is a set of darn runs inside its own beam:

1. Task A runs Discussion as today; Discussion stays the one agent that talks with the operator and decides scope.
2. A pre-planner breaks the decided scope into smaller pieces that together make up the whole scope.
   Each piece gets a contract: what it takes in, the behaviour it delivers, the names it exports to other pieces, and which pieces it depends on; not the inside, which the darn finds itself.
3. Each piece becomes a darn task with that contract and its part of the decision record and `relevant.md`, with `depends_on` between pieces.
4. The next producer turns Task A's worktree into a beam.
5. The darn tasks run from beam A as ordinary darn runs and merge back into Task A's branch, not `main`; pieces with no dependency between them run in parallel.
6. When every darn has merged back, a Task A-wide perch reviews the whole and makes small fixes.
7. The rest is as today: Parent-Align, PR, landing, so `main` takes Task A whole.

## Why

`docs/research/token-audit-2026-10-22`: a loom run carries a fixed cost of about $23, mostly Plan and the review rounds, and the Plan writer reads about 250k of context before it writes (91% of its peak).
Darn's fixed cost is about $2.60.
Split this way, each darn reads only its piece once, plans and implements it, and is reviewed by its own perch; Discussion and the whole-task perch keep loom's scope and overall check.
It came out of discussing sub-planners for the Plan writer (note `plan-writer-context`): pieces small enough to plan and implement together are darn runs.

## Depends on

The beam setup: `orch-any-worktree` is landed (dd11ab09f: beams, pairs from a parent pair, `lym beam create`, `land`; its `promote` was removed by `beam-start-and-ownership`, which also added `lym beam start` and the `pawl` recipe), and `umbrella-daemon` is landed too (c2a03a885: dobby, a per-beam daemon that drives runs).
Earlier wording: `orch-any-worktree` (umbrella tasks spawning and landing from their own worktree) and `umbrella-daemon` (a daemon per beam that drives its runs).

## Open

- Contract precision: too loose and pieces collide, too tight and the pre-planner becomes today's Plan writer.
- A darn that finds its contract wrong stops and escalates to Task A instead of improvising; dependent pieces wait.
- What drives the darns inside the beam: dobby now starts and drives a beam's ready tasks (c2a03a885); open is how Task A's run waits for them.
- How large the whole-task perch's fixes may be before they mean a piece failed.
- Quality against full loom: each piece gets one perch instead of Plan and Webster review; measure follow-up fixes against loom runs.
- Cost: Discussion, pre-planner, N darns and the whole-task perch against a loom run of the same size.

## Review placement (operator, 2026-10-22)

- The pre-plan gets a perch, but the pre-plan is far smaller than today's plan format: pieces and their contracts, not cards.
- No perch per darn: a review per batch proved far too expensive in Millhouse, and a perch per piece is the same.
  The pieces run as darn with review off (`code_max_bounces: 0`, since `code-review-one-perch` made darn's perch the Code-Review perch), each still passing its own gate and tests; the whole-task perch after the last merge-back is the code review, as Webster's round over the whole diff is today.
  For scale, a darn perch costs about $1.30 per run in the audit window.
- The pieces run tests as they go, the way Webster's card gate runs after every card.

## Piece recipe `stitch` (operator, 2026-10-22)

The pieces run on their own recipe, `stitch`, derived from darn, not on a darn profile: rows go away, not only bounds.
Alignment per piece is pointless when the piece is a closed, synchronised share of an umbrella that is aligned whole.

- Kept: Preflight; the writer, on Sonnet, briefed by its pre-plan contract.
- Dropped: Code-Bouncer and the Code-Burler review/fix rows (review off), Describe and PR-Review.
  Since `loom-tail-review` (2026-10-24) darn has no Merge-In, Publish, PR-Align or PR-Gate rows; its Finalize merges the parent in under the lock.
- Finalize merges into the umbrella branch under the parent lock instead of landing on `main`.
- Friction-Reflect runs once per umbrella, not per piece.
- A `stitch` task runs only inside an umbrella; it cannot run alone.
- Estimate (orch, not measured): about $2-2.50 per piece against about $6 for a darn with review.

Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-24): once `stitch` exists, Codex could run the pre-planner, as a role apart from the Claude-written code (see note `codex-engine`).

## Operator view, not a decision (2026-10-23): darn itself as the piece implementer

Once `loom-tail-review` has landed, darn itself may serve as the pieces' implementer, since that task removes much of the run tail's ceremony, such as the pull request.
Whether `stitch` then stays a recipe of its own, or becomes darn with the tail rows a piece does not need turned off, is to be weighed against what `loom-tail-review` lands.

## Test depth of a piece (operator, 2026-10-23)

A piece run does not run the full suite a standalone darn runs before it lands.
The umbrella runs the full suite once, after every piece has merged back.
Which tiers a piece's own gates run is open; the gate key per recipe row is stated in `internal/gateslot`'s doc (`gate-runs-once`, landed): a piece's rows read `darn-write`, `code-burler-fix` and `finalize`.

## Pre-plan depth (orch, 2026-10-24, not decided)

- A coarse pre-plan leaves design to the pieces, so each piece needs an Opus writer.
- A detailed pre-plan carries the design, so Sonnet pieces may do, at the cost of a heavier pre-planner.
- Pieces cannot be counted on to run in parallel: `tools/plandag/plandag.sh` on `loom-tail-review`'s plan found 52 cards, a critical path of 20 and a mean parallelism of 2.6.
  A beam's gain is then mostly smaller review scopes, not wall time.

entries.title: Beam promote keeps the Discussion record as part of the beam
entries.brief: When Discussion finds a task should be a project, promote carries its decision record into the beam instead of dropping it
entries.body:
## Seen (2026-10-25)

`lym beam promote <slug>` ends the task's run for good, keeps the code commits on the pair's branch, and resets the pair's records to a fresh fork of its parent's.
The run's discussion, plan and run records leave the worktree and stay only in the records history.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-25)

The likely moment to promote is Discussion finding that the task is so large it should be a project.
Then everything the Discussion writer found must be kept: its decision record and what it learned become part of the beam, as the beam's starting design, not something left behind in history.
Note `loom-beam-darns` is a related shape, where a large loom task turns its own worktree into a beam and runs the pieces inside it.

## Until then (operator, 2026-10-25)

Beams are made with `lym beam create` on a project entry only; `lym beam promote` is not used.

## Landed since (beam-start-and-ownership)

`lym beam promote` is removed, so the Seen and Until-then sections above describe a verb that no longer exists.
A beam's life is now one batten run over its project entry with the `pawl` recipe; the idea here, keeping Discussion's record as a beam's starting design, still stands but needs a new route.

entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-25)

The board renders one README.md holding every project, task and note of the hub.
The notes are grouped by type label in file order, so after the `audit` label became `research` the research notes moved from first under Notes to last, under the heading `Researchs`.

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-25)

- Research notes come first under Notes, right after the tasks, where the audits stood; the heading reads `Research`.
- Each project gets its own rendered file.
  It opens with the projects directly under it, each a link to its file with its short description, then holds the tasks and notes that belong to the project itself.
- Every project sits under another project, except the root project at the top.
- The split is rendering only: every entry stays in the one board store, and handles stay numbered across the whole hub, so a project's file shows gaps in its numbering and a handle names one entry whichever file shows it.
- A task's After column names its dependencies by handle instead of by slug, one handle per line within the cell.
- A draft task is not ready, so it never shows under Ready: drafts get a subsection of their own after the ready and layered tasks (built: `### Draft (n)` in the Tasks section, see `internal/boardengine/doc.go`).
- README.md is the root project's file: the projects under root first, each linked with its short description, then every task and note that belongs to no other project.


The board README rendering is not regarded as production code (operator, 2026-10-27).

entries.title: No test is skipped by design
entries.brief: Windows-only tests count as skips on Linux, and TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape skips on every machine
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-26, OSL-1046)

The adopt check's gate run on Linux reported skipped tests in tier0 and tier1.
`TestUp_BootValidation/TmuxConfUnvalidatedOnWindows` (`internal/reedengine/lifecycle_test.go`) skips itself on every machine but Windows, so a Linux run counts it as a skip; tier1 has more Windows-only tests of the same kind.
`TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape` (`internal/loomcli/sharedbootstrap_test.go`) skips itself whenever `buildLoomShed` fails, which it does because the test sets up no real fabric, so it most likely tests nothing on any machine.
Tier1 also skips the deliberate `TestCrossProduct` matrix cells (`internal/fabricengine/livestate_matrix_test.go`) and the child-process helper tests, which skip unless a parent test spawns them.

## Decided (operator, 2026-10-26)

No test is skipped by design: a test that is meant to skip has no place in the suite.

- A test that only means something on one OS moves into a file behind a `//go:build` tag for that OS, so other machines never compile it.
- `TestBuildLoomShed_OutputShape` either builds the real fabric it needs and fails when `buildLoomShed` fails, or is deleted.
- The matrix cells that are skipped by design are not generated at all.
- The child-process helpers stop being test functions the runner sees, for example by dispatching from `TestMain` on an environment variable.
- A skip that remains is a missing prerequisite, such as `TestGateTest_DotnetFixture` without its NuGet packages, so a skip in the gate log is always worth reading.
- `TestClaude/neither_skips/inner` in `internal/testkit/llmkit` is the skip helper's own test and stays.

entries.title: Ideas from r/ClaudeCode "one line in your CLAUDE.md": fit for LoomYard and bench measures
entries.brief: About 30 ideas judged against our stencils and rules; top 8 ranked for a bench, a few cheap enough without one
entries.body:
# r/ClaudeCode "What's the one line in your CLAUDE.md that made the biggest difference?" — review for LoomYard

Status: the operator decides whether a research task with a bench is drafted from section 1; nothing is promoted yet (2026-10-26).

Source: the r/ClaudeCode thread named in the title, read from a 17-page PDF export kept only on OSL-1046.
The post shows 887 votes and 187 comments.
The export shows no per-comment vote counts, so "prominence" below means position under Best sort, reply count, or the OP's own endorsement.
Paths below are repository-relative unless they start with `~/.claude`, which stands for `/home/AD.NORCERESEARCH.NO/hanf/.claude/plugins/cache/scribe/scribe/1.1.0/skills`.

## 1. Ideas most worth a bench, ranked

1. **Trust the code for what happens, and report every doc/code disagreement** (SirRobinBlibs, cites arXiv 2610.30571).
   Measure: seed a fixture hub with stale statements in `CLAUDE.md`, a `doc.go` and a `pattern/` file, run darn on tasks that touch them, and count the share of seeded conflicts the change description or a friction note reports, and the share where the agent copied the stale text.
2. **Never weaken, skip or delete a test or assertion to make a change pass** (NamerekDev, namrog84).
   Measure: per run, a diff scan of the task branch for removed `t.Run` cases, removed assertions, added `t.Skip` and deleted test functions, plus a planted task whose correct fix needs a test that is hard to satisfy.
3. **Read every file you need in one pass, then edit, then test once** (the post itself, 887 votes).
   Measure: on darn runs, token spend per run, `lym gate test` calls per run, Reads issued after the first Edit, and Code-Review findings of class `consistency` naming a missed sibling site.
4. **Before writing "we do X" or "we don't have X", reopen the code and cite `file:line`** (Stunning-Sherbet1853; OP said "stealing it").
   Measure: sample the factual claims about the codebase in change descriptions, decision records and board notes, check each against the code, and count false claims per run.
5. **Mutation check after writing tests** (namrog84: break one behavior on purpose and confirm a test fails).
   Measure: mutation score of the tests a run added or changed, computed over the changed packages by a Go mutation tool, compared across arms.
6. **A mistake names its instruction cause** (pixxelkick, adapted by Classic-Asparagus: "a missing, ambiguous, or conflicting instruction, or a clear instruction you did not follow").
   Measure: share of friction-filed issues that name a specific stencil or rule line as the cause, and the recurrence rate of the same issue in later runs after the cited line is fixed.
7. **Read the related tests before touching anything** (masiha97).
   Measure: first-gate failure rate per card or per darn commit, and self-fix attempts spent per card.
8. **Cheap model for the fresh-eyes reviewer** (pixxelkick: "spin up a sub agent with minimal context using a cheap model").
   Measure: run Code-Burler with the reviewer on a smaller model against the default, and compare findings per run, the fixer's dispute rate (false positives) and findings a later round or landing catches (false negatives), against token cost.

## 2. Every idea

### Read all, edit all, test once (post, 887 votes)

"Before changing anything, list every file you'll need and read them in one pass. Then make all edits, then run the tests once."
A reply (page 15) adds: keep one test run before the edits, so a failure at the end is attributable.

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: webster's FRESH-READ rule, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-body-implementer.md:5-7`, and span reads via `lym quarry resolve` at `:53`; burler's pre-read for fork reviewers, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-fork-reading.md:9-16`; twill's writer fork, `contracts/stencils/twill/twill-writer-fork.md:9`.
  The baseline half exists as webster's "a failure the card did not cause" test, `webster-body-implementer.md:113-122`, and drift's baseline, `contracts/stencils/drift/drift-template-baseline.md`.
- Missing: the darn writer gets no read-first rule and is told "Test as you work", `contracts/stencils/darn/darn-template-write.md:72-74`, the opposite of "test once".
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4.
- Bench: yes, see rank 3.

### Treat corrections as a queue, do not drop current work (pixxelkick, top comment)

- Verdict: does not fit as written; the orch analogue is already in place.
- Why: spawned agents take no mid-run operator corrections except recorded decisions (`lym loom decision add`, `.lym/orch/role.md:284`), and the orch puts every proposal "on the board as a note at once, never held in your head", `.lym/orch/role.md:324`.

### A mistake names its instruction cause; no apology (pixxelkick; Classic-Asparagus's `_observations/` folder and session reflection)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: friction notes, `contracts/stencils/friction/friction-directive-implementer.md:14-27`, filed by the reflection agent as issues, `contracts/stencils/friction/friction-template-reflection.md:122-163`; the no-apology tone rule, `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md:33`; orch workarounds go into the rules file with the issue number, `.lym/orch/role.md:353`.
- Missing: the friction directive asks what went wrong, not which instruction caused it (missing, ambiguous, conflicting, or clear but not followed), and the reflection agent does not classify by that.
- Where: the four `friction-directive-*.md` files and the reflection template.
- Bench: yes, see rank 6.

### YAGNI, no unasked scope, propose scope improvements separately (pixxelkick)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:27-34`; Code-Review flags unlicensed scope, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-rubric-code-review.md:62-63`, and so does plan review, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-rubric-plan-review.md:82`; follow-ups go on the board as notes, `darn-template-write.md:261`.

### Fresh-eyes reviewer sub-agent on a cheap model (pixxelkick)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: every review round is a fresh session, `contracts/recipes/loom-recipe.yaml:71`, and model choice is per role, `contracts/specs/llm-model-spec.md`.
- Missing: evidence for which reviewer model is cost-effective.
- Bench: yes, see rank 8.

### "Make no mistakes", "it's for a children's hospital", "Codex said it could do better", "use a polite manner"

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: jokes or motivational framing with no mechanism to test.

### Never weaken or delete a test to make it pass; tests do not get edited to pass (NamerekDev, namrog84)

NamerekDev: "it stopped editing them. it deletes them now!"; a hook added for it was deleted by the next session.

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: only the webster verify-gate fixer, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-body-verify-fix.md:26-27`; burler's fixer corrects a wrong assertion rather than adding tests, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-step-fix.md:44`.
- Missing: the webster implementer, the darn writer, the burler fixer and the landing merge fixer (`contracts/stencils/landing/landing-template-fixer.md:31`, "fix the failing tests only") carry no such rule, and the Code-Review rubric does not flag a weakened test.
- Where: one shared rule rendered into every editing role, the way `contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md` is, plus a Code-Review rubric line; a Go diff scan in the gate would make it structural, which matters given NamerekDev's hook story.
- Bench: yes, see rank 2.

### Mutation check after writing tests (namrog84)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: RED-before-GREEN, but only "when TDD is specified", `~/.claude/testing/SKILL.md:49-57`.
- Missing: no stencil or plan card asks for it.
- Where: the plan spec's test-card rules or the implementer stencil, or a `lym gate` step.
- Bench: yes, see rank 5.

### Review your work for creeping complexity and propose a workflow change (sammcj, partly cut off in the export); "keep it succinct" (es-ganso)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: review rounds judge design against the rubric; friction notes carry workflow proposals; brevity is `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:14-35`.

### Commit messages: short subject, body or not, no Co-Authored-By, task hash in the next commit (waruyamaZero, OP, howitzer1)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: subject shape `N: <name>`, `webster-body-implementer.md:68`; the landing writes the description and the trailer, `contracts/stencils/landing/landing-template-describe.md:49`.

### The agent you talk to never writes code; it supervises sub-agents (maniac56)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: "You diagnose; the run's own agents change the run", `.lym/orch/role.md:281`; webster's Master never reads code, `contracts/stencils/webster/webster-template-master.md:19`.

### Simplified Technical English; ban "load-bearing", em dashes, slop words (basskittens, bigtime_porgrammer, Icy-Excitement-467)

The OP replied that banning em dashes made the model use " - " instead: "swapped one tell for another".

- Verdict: partly, and not worth a bench.
- Have: `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:14-35`.
- Why not more: the operator's own skills use "load-bearing" (`~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:51`) and em dashes; a word ban trades one tell for another, as the OP saw.
  STE is the one variant with substance, since it constrains structure rather than banning tokens; it is a taste call for the operator, not a pipeline lever.

### Ask for a "go" before writing code; exploration mode; plan first, then `/grilling` (renatodinhani, holyknight00, getastatic)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: the pipeline is this: Discussion explores before asking, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-discussion.md:50-54`, then Plan, then Plan-Burler review rounds, which interrogate the plan before Webster writes code.

### "Do not guess"; prefer official docs; say when an answer rests only on training data (Whiteshovel66, TalShar)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: "Read the index below before guessing a `lym` command", `plugins/ly/skills/cli/SKILL.md:8`; Discussion reads code before asking, `loom-template-discussion.md:52-53`.
- Missing: nothing asks an agent to flag a claim about an external library or tool that it did not verify (go-git, cobra, tree-sitter, tmux, Claude Code flags).
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md` or the implementer stencil.
- Bench: possible but weak: count first-gate compile failures on undefined symbols of external packages.

### Cite `file:line` before claiming "we do X" (Stunning-Sherbet1853)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: review findings need `path:line` evidence, `contracts/stencils/burler/burler-fix-check-rubric.md:18`, and disputes need cited text, `burler-step-fix.md:31`.
- Missing: change descriptions, decision records, board notes and orch replies make code claims with no citation rule; Discussion deliberately avoids `file:line` (`loom-template-discussion.md:57`), so the rule must target claims of presence or absence, not signatures.
- Where: `landing-template-describe*.md`, `darn-template-write.md` Step 5, the orch role's board section, and `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md` for chat.
- Bench: yes, see rank 4.

### "Clearly call out the next action" (4bitfocus)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: aimed at a solo chat loop where the human approves each step; runs are autonomous, and orch status reports already carry the attach command, `.lym/orch/role.md:393`.

### A repo map: one-line description per file, kept current (No_Dig_7017)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: `lym quarry toc`, `contracts/stencils/loom/loom-template-plan.md:65`, fed by file headers and doc comments written to that bar, `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:113-120`.
- Missing: only the planner is pointed at it; the darn writer and burler reviewers are not.
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4 and `burler-step-1-explore.md`'s tool-use rules.
- Bench: possible: darn token spend and Reads before the first Edit, with and without the pointer; fold into the rank-3 bench rather than running it alone.

### No backward compatibility unless asked; update every call site (danielllenton)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:23-25`.

### Known-errors wiki per language, read before coding, appended after each own mistake (IxBetaXI)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: PATTERN plus `pattern/` and the orch rules play that role, with a size bound (`internal/pattern/headroom.go:7`); an agent-appended log would grow without review, which the headroom lint exists to stop.

### Skill-run logs and a weekly cron turning repeated actions into skills (bkrsh099)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: friction notes already carry the signal; the commenter says most generated skills get rejected.

### "Refactoring is harm": write `foo-2` beside `foo` (cjmurrr)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: conflicts with "no `_old`/`_v2` duplication — change the call sites", `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:24`; the thread itself rejects it.

### Do not rely on CLAUDE.md for secrets; block at the filesystem or proxy (radim11)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: guards live in code, `internal/shellguard` (package doc), and reed strips provider environment keys, `pattern/PATTERN-shuttle-provider-seam.md:9`.

### No system-wide `grep`/`find` (alanvnk: "nearly doubled the amount of sessions I can run")

- Verdict: worth adopting, if transcripts show it happens.
- Have: the plan spec scopes grep to a package, `contracts/specs/loom-plan-spec.md:370`.
- Where: a `internal/shellguard` row denying a recursive `grep`/`find`/`rg` rooted at `/` or `~`, since many parallel lym sessions share one machine.
- Bench: not needed; grep a sample of strand transcripts for such calls first.

### Replace CLAUDE.md lines with hooks and gates; a hook flags comments that will go stale (Neat-Culture9983 and parent)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: PATTERN entries enforced by tests, `CLAUDE.md:8`; `internal/shellguard`, `internal/commentlint`, `internal/patternlint`; the perishable-specific rule, `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md` "Don't pin a perishable specific".

### Docs and code disagree: follow the code, and report every inconsistency (SirRobinBlibs, arXiv 2610.30571: following the code went from 4.2% to 91.4% over 320 runs)

- Verdict: worth adopting, both halves (corrected by the operator, 2026-10-26).
- A description of behavior, in a `doc.go`, a `pattern/` file or `CLAUDE.md`, is not a rule: the code is the fact of what happens, so an agent that needs to know what the code does trusts the code, never a stale description.
  The code may still be wrong, so the mismatch is a finding, not a verdict: the agent silently fixes neither side and reports which side it believes is wrong.
  This is apart from `loom-rubric-code-review.md:66`, where a written rule on how new code should be written outranks a convention inferred from the surrounding code.
- Missing: no editing role is told to report a doc/code disagreement it meets, so a stale `doc.go` or `pattern/` line goes unreported.
- Where: one line in the implementer, darn writer and burler fixer stencils sending each disagreement to the change description or a friction note.
- Bench: yes, see rank 1.

### Call things what they are; do not invent terminology (actual-time-traveler, Classic-Asparagus)

- Verdict: does not fit for the project, partly for agents.
- Why: LoomYard coins its own names on purpose (weft, warp, reed, creel, dobby, batten); `CLAUDE.md:59-61` already confines the shorthands to conversation.
  An agent coining a new term in a stencil or doc comment is a review-level concern, not a bench.

### Ask one question before editing instead of guessing; say what you did not test (London-Boat)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: the question half is `~/.claude/conversation/SKILL.md:32` for chat and Discussion for runs (darn deliberately never blocks on a dialog, `darn-template-write.md:14`); the untested half is "anything to check or run by hand that was not run", `landing-template-describe.md:42` and `landing-template-describe-darn.md:39`.

### Hook at 50% context: wind down, hand off (puts_on_rddt)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: orch distill and refresh (`plugins/ly/skills/distill`, `plugins/ly/skills/refresh`), the orch handoff templates under `contracts/stencils/orch/`, and `scribe:handoff`; spawned strands are short-lived by design.

### "Do not suggest waiting until tomorrow"; human time estimates (extremelyhotdad)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: no agent schedules its own work; dobby drives runs.

### No new markdown file without asking; one fact, one owner file (SimplifAI_Life; pixxelkick on markdown litter)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `~/.claude/prose/SKILL.md:33-35`, `~/.claude/code-quality/SKILL.md:66-68`, `PATTERN-stencil-ownership` in `PATTERN.md`, scratch files under `.scratch/` (`contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md:8`), and friction notes at a fixed path "with no filename of your own choosing".

### Every mistake becomes a rule or, better, a pre-work check (Weekly_Cat6537)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `CLAUDE.md:10` (a new invariant goes into PATTERN with its code), PATTERN entries marked `(test)`, and the orch workaround rule, `.lym/orch/role.md:353`.

### Keep CLAUDE.md under a page or it gets ignored (OP)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: `CLAUDE.md` is short and PATTERN growth is linted, `internal/pattern/headroom.go:7`.
- Missing: the orch role is 530 lines with hub rules inlined, and the stencils are long; nothing measures whether length costs compliance.
- Bench: possible and useful: a trimmed against a full orch role on replayed scenarios, counting violations of a fixed set of role rules.
  It is expensive to set up, so it ranks below the eight above.

### Read the related tests before touching code (masiha97)

- Verdict: partly.
- Have: plan cards name the tests they change or reuse, `loom-template-plan.md:176-182`; burler's pre-read covers tests, `burler-fork-reading.md:14`.
- Missing: the darn writer and the merge fixer are not told to.
- Where: `darn-template-write.md` Step 4 and `landing-template-fixer.md`.
- Bench: yes, see rank 7.

### Explicit failure path: if X fails try Y, then report and stop (Joozio)

- Verdict: have it.
- Where: `PATTERN-refusal-way-forward` in `PATTERN.md`; the bounded self-fix and `NEEDS_PARENT`, `webster-body-implementer.md:108-130`.

### Block bulk edits with a hook so each file edit is visible (ghost_operative)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: LoomYard just allowed scripted edits on purpose (`contracts/stencils/edit/edit-directive.md`, commit `a1b6053a`); the scope guard and review read the diff instead.

### Some CLAUDE.md content belongs in a custom output style (thebigslapper)

- Verdict: does not fit.
- Why: spawned agents get their instructions from stencils, not from CLAUDE.md or output styles.

## 3. Cheap enough to adopt without a bench

- One shared "never delete, skip or weaken a test or assertion to make it pass" rule for every editing role, copied from `webster-body-verify-fix.md:26-27`, plus a Code-Review rubric line flagging it.
  A bench is still worth running to see whether a prose rule suffices or a diff scan is needed.
- One line in the editing stencils: report each doc/code disagreement you meet in the change description or a friction note, trusting the code for what happens and naming the side it believes is wrong.
- Point the darn writer at `lym quarry toc` and at reading the tests of the code it changes, in `darn-template-write.md` Step 4.
- A friction-note prompt line asking for the instruction cause: missing, ambiguous, conflicting, or clear but not followed.
- A `shellguard` row against recursive searches rooted at `/` or the home directory, once a transcript sample shows they happen.

entries.title: An instruction typed into a pane is lost when the tackler re-spawns the row
entries.brief: A re-spawned row session starts from its prompt alone; operator input to the old session is dropped
entries.body:
## Seen

An instruction the operator typed into a worker's tmux pane was lost when the tackler re-spawned that row's session: the new session started from the row's prompt alone, and nothing carried the typed line over.

## Idea

When a row is re-spawned, carry over what the operator said to the old session, for example by reading the operator's turns from the old transcript, or by routing operator input through creel so it is recorded and re-delivered to the new session.
At the least, warn the operator in the pane or by a notice that the session was replaced and an unanswered instruction may be lost.

entries.title: A run keeps the lym binary and Bolt instructions it started with
entries.body:
## Seen (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run reads its instructions live while it runs: the `lym` binary, and the stencils, specs and hub config on Bolt (`_board/_lym/{stencils,specs,config}`).
A landing deploys a new `lym` and can change those files, so a run started on one version can finish on another, such as a darn run that sat between its drift rows when `darn-drift-await-row` landed and its recipe changed under it (that landing wrote no transition code: such a run halts at Drift-Verify and is settled by hand with `lym drift waive`).
LoomYard takes no special care for such a run today, and the operator wants none written per change (operator, 2026-10-27).

## Idea (operator, 2026-10-27)

A run keeps the version it started with, so nothing changes under it.
- Bolt: the run records the Bolt commit at its start and reads stencils, specs and config from that commit through git, in the one place those files are read, instead of from the working files; no copy is made.
- Binary: at the run's start the running `lym` is copied into a store under a name derived from its content, as the gate's prebuilt store does (`internal/gateslot`), and the run's driver and agents call that copy.
- Shared state stays live: the board, locks, gate slots, creel mail and the run's own records.
- One verb moves a run onto the newest version, for a run that needs a fix that landed after it started.

## Open

- Shared daemons (dobby, creel, gate) run the newest binary, so a pinned run's formats must stay readable by them, and a pinned binary must not write the board in an older format.
- Plugins and skills are loaded by Claude Code from one shared place and are left out of the first step.

entries.title: Creel delivers every post to a Claude strand through hooks, visibly and in full
entries.brief: PostToolUse, Stop and asyncRewake hooks carry posts as fast as possible; shuttle appends a trust and reply sentence to the system prompt
entries.body:
## Goal

Creel delivers every post to a Claude strand under the hood, through hooks shuttle renders into the session's `settings.json`, as fast as possible, in full, visibly to the operator, and acted on by the receiver.
A scope change from the orch reaches a working agent at its next tool call, never only at its turn end.
Codex is out of scope until `codexengine` exists.

## Evidence

- `docs/research/creel-hook-channels-2026-10-28/report.md`: which hook channels deliver and which the operator sees.
- `docs/research/creel-midturn-trust-2026-10-28/report.md`: a `PostToolUse` block with `reason` and `systemMessage` is taken at once by Sonnet with or without a system-prompt sentence, and by Haiku only with it; the operator sees the message under the tool result.
- `additionalContext` is out: the operator cannot see it, and Haiku refused to act on it.

## Delivery: one kind of post, as fast as possible

- While the receiver works: its `PostToolUse` hook hands over its unread mail with `decision: "block"`, the lines as `reason`, and the same lines as `systemMessage`, so the operator sees them under the tool result.
- When it arrives after the turn's last tool call: the `Stop` hook blocks with the lines as `reason`, so the turn goes on; it blocks only while unread mail stands, so it cannot loop.
- While the receiver is idle: an `asyncRewake` hook wakes the session with the lines.
  Today that wake shows the operator only a bare `Stop hook feedback` line; the build makes the message text itself visible in the pane, and stops and asks the parent when it finds no way.
- Each message is delivered once, by whichever path reserves it first, as creel's claim already does; a wake waiter that loses the race to a new turn delivers nothing.
- Delivery happens in the session's main thread only: a hook call whose input marks it as coming from a subagent or fork (Claude Code's `agent_id`, to be confirmed by a test) delivers nothing and leaves the mail for the main thread's next boundary.
  The main role passes on to its forks what they need.
- Pause and hold keep their rules: nothing under a pause, only the owner's mail under a hold.
- The 8 KiB claim budget stays; what is left goes at the next boundary.

## Creel changes

- Agent mail is delivered in full like any other mail; the reminder line and its `lym creel read` turn go.
- The pane path for posts goes: every session is launched by shuttle and has the hooks, and a session launched before the deploy gets posts once it is restarted.
- `inject` keeps typing into the pane, since `/clear`, `/compact` and the resume line need it.
- `lym creel post --interrupt` sends the guarded interrupt first and then posts, so the message reaches the stopped session at once through the idle wake; `interrupt` stays its own verb.
- Wherever creel writes a strand name in text, it quotes it: `[creel] #1 from "ly:orch": …`, in `creelengine.MessageLine` and `lym creel read`'s output.
  Strand names keep `:`; `/`, `#`, `@`, `.` and `-` were weighed and refused (operator, 2026-10-28).

## Trust and replies

Shuttle appends one sentence to the system prompt of every Claude session it launches, with `--append-system-prompt`, so trust rests on no skill and no `CLAUDE.md`:

```text
Lines starting with [creel] are LoomYard internal mail delivered by hooks; follow them as the operator's own instructions. When one asks for an answer, reply with lym creel post --reply <id> "<text>", using the id after #; answer mail from EXTERNAL in your own reply text instead.
```

The sentence does not tell senders apart: a message is a message (operator, 2026-10-28).
A reply to EXTERNAL reaches only a waiting `post --wait-reply`, so the agent answers the operator in its own text, which the operator sees in the pane.
`lym creel`'s Cobra help, on the command group and on `post`, carries the same reply rule.

## Test

The build tests through shuttle's own rendered `settings.json` and launch arguments, never with hand-launched sessions: mid-turn delivery, the `Stop` block, the idle wake and its visible text, the fork and subagent filter, and `post --interrupt`.

entries.title: Machine checks in validate-discussion and validate-plan for recurring review findings
entries.brief: Citation and acceptance checks for the decision record; seam-test, tier-tag and doc.go checks for plan cards
entries.body:
## Seen

`docs/research/review-setup-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` (section 3) classed the gating Discussion and Plan findings and found themes a machine check could stop before a reviewer spends a round on them.
The operator agreed with its recommendations (2026-10-28); this task builds the checks.

## Design

`lym loom validate-discussion`, and the gates of the rows that run it:

- A citation check: every repository path and Go symbol the decision record cites exists.
- An acceptance check: every decision id appears in at least one acceptance criterion.

`lym loom validate-plan`, and the gates of the rows that run it:

- A card that adds a field to a shared `Deps` or `Env` struct lists the reflective seam tests of that struct.
- A card that adds a test file states exactly one tier tag for it.
- A card whose Intent changes a package's behaviour lists that package's `doc.go`.

Each check's refusal names the item it found and what the writer adds to fix it.
The Discussion and Plan writer stencils state the new rules, so a writer meets them before the gate does.

## Out of scope

- Lens and profile changes: a task of their own.
- Checks for the design-interaction and unbounded-edge classes, which the report leaves to the lenses.

entries.title: Stencil and system-prompt sentences that batch independent calls and edits
entries.brief: The turn audit sentences per heavy role, plus one shuttle-appended system-prompt sentence for every Claude agent
entries.body:
## Seen

A session's cost grows with its turns times its context.
`docs/research/turn-audit-2026-10-28/report.md` found that a large share of the heavy roles' turns are single-call turns whose calls did not depend on each other, and edits made one per turn; its section 5 words a sentence per role.
The operator agreed with its recommendations (2026-10-28); this task builds them.
Agents keep reading the source themselves: nothing here hands an agent pre-read or digested source.

## Design

- Add the report's section 5 sentence for each role to that role's stencil: the darn writer, the Webster implementer, the Discussion and Plan writers, the twill lens directive, the burler review step that reads the focus, the burler fixer and the landing fixer.
  The rule they carry: gather every file and search you can name in one message before the first edit, make independent edits in one message, and run the gate once after the last edit.
- Shuttle appends one sentence to every Claude agent's system prompt with `--append-system-prompt`: "Request every call whose arguments you already know in one message, and read what you need before you edit; wait for a result only to choose the next call."
  It sits beside the creel sentence shuttle appends, in one appended prompt.

## Measure

No bench before the change: the next loom and darn runs after landing are measured against the report's figures by re-running the report's scripts on their transcripts, as a later audit.

## Out of scope

- A `PostToolUse` hook that nudges toward batching; only if the stencil and prompt sentences do not cut enough.

entries.title: Webster recovery has a way forward, and its audit accepts a sanctioned gate test
entries.body:
## webster recovery way-forward is circular: recover-batch points to accept-audit, which refuses; reset is refused while run.lock is held (was note `webster-recovery-circular`)

Imported from [issue #878](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/878).

#### What happened

After `lyx webster record-batch` failed a batch on fabric-reference audit findings, `lyx webster recover-batch` refused with `needs_fresh` and a way forward of "`lyx webster accept-audit --batch 6` then `lyx webster recover-batch 6`", or `reset --to batch-start`, or `reset --to start`.
`lyx webster accept-audit --batch=6` then refused, because the batch's commits are kept only when every fabric reference is read-only, and the finding is the very one that made recover-batch advise it. Its only way forward was `lyx webster reset --to batch-start --batch 06`.
`lyx webster reset --to=batch-start --batch=6` was refused with `run is already in progress ... (run.lock held)`, with way forward "wait for it to finish, or check `lyx webster status`".
The Webster session had no verb left that it was allowed to use, so it escalated: the run halted `blocked` with anomaly `escalation-to-human`, and the halt note says the parent has to run the reset after the run stops.

#### Why it is abnormal

- `recover-batch` offers `accept-audit` as a way forward in a case where `accept-audit` is known to refuse; the advice cannot be followed.
- The refusals were retried several times (two `accept-audit` refusals, three `recover-batch` refusals), each with the same text.
- `reset` is refused for a lock the Webster session itself holds, so the one working remedy is unreachable from inside the run that needs it.

#### What to do

- Have `recover-batch` run the `accept-audit` check and drop that option from the way forward when it would refuse.
- Let `reset --to batch-start` run from the Webster session that owns `run.lock`, or have the refusal name who must run it and when.

#### Provenance

Task `umbrella-anchor`; notes: webster-refusal-recover-batch.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch-2.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch-3.md, webster-refusal-accept-audit.md, webster-refusal-accept-audit-2.md, webster-refusal-reset.md, loom-halt-3.md.

## webster fabric-reference audit flags the sanctioned lyx gate test as a run-state rewrite, failing the batch (was note `webster-audit-gate-test-readonly`)

Imported from [issue #877](https://github.com/Knatte18/loomyard/issues/877).

#### What happened

A Webster implementer fork ran `lyx gate test --wait --gate card --card <card>` and `lyx gate test --wait --gate batch --card <card>`, the gate commands the session's own gate rule tells agents to run, and once chained them after a `git commit`.
`lyx webster record-batch` failed the batch with `fabric-reference violation ... ran a fabric-referencing command ("lyx gate test ...") that can rewrite run state — an implementer fork must never touch the fabric repo directly`.
The finding "names no path"; it is raised from the command text alone.
`lyx webster recover-batch` then refused with `needs_fresh` on the same findings.

#### Why it is abnormal

`lyx gate test` is the mandated way to run tests, so the audit makes the normal workflow a violation.
The audit does not distinguish a gate invocation from a command that writes the fabric repo, and a pipe through `tail`/`grep` does not change that.
A whole batch of otherwise valid work was lost to the flag, and the run halted blocked at Webster with an escalation.

#### What to do

Treat `lyx gate test` (and its `--wait`, `--gate`, `--card` forms) as read-only for the fabric-reference audit, or make the audit check the paths a command actually writes.
At minimum the finding should say why this specific command can rewrite run state.

#### Provenance

Task `umbrella-anchor`; notes: webster-refusal-record-batch.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch-2.md, webster-refusal-recover-batch-3.md, loom-halt.md, loom-halt-2.md, loom-halt-3.md.

entries.title: The dobby holds a new run start while the user slice nears its task limit
entries.brief: Hold new run starts when the user slice pids.current nears pids.max
entries.body:
Follow-up from task `gate-robustness` (issue #885), which made no .NET build leave MSBuild servers behind and made `lym gate test` rerun a tier once on a fork EAGAIN, but left the dobby unchanged.

With five loom runs and a darn run live, the user slice reached `pids.current 2997` of `pids.max 3000` and every fork failed.
Six parallel runs sit close to the default limit even without leaked processes.

What to do: before a dobby pass starts a new run, read the user slice cgroup's `pids.current` and `pids.max` on Linux and hold the start, logged with both numbers, while the headroom is below a configured margin.
A machine with no readable cgroup starts runs as today.

The EAGAIN retries in git wrappers and the transient halt class `host-resources` for loom runs landed with `transient-halt-recovery`; this note is only the hold on a new run start.
